title: Watching Neurons Light Up
endLine: Calcium imaging turns calcium changes into light to track neural activity.

scenes.tts: Which of these neurons just fired? Their shapes give little away. But watch what happens when the cells contain a protein that changes how brightly it glows. Now there is a change we can follow.
scenes.caption: Which of these neurons just fired? Their shapes give little away. But watch what happens when the cells contain a protein that changes how brightly it glows. Now there is a change we can follow.
scenes.visual: Open immediately on a schematic microscope field with a few full-height neuron outlines and slowly moving focal illumination. Pose the question in voice over the field. When the voice introduces the protein, bring its faint green glow into view in the cells, then let one cell brighten as the centre of attention. Keep the same field through the title. Throughout, fill most of the frame height with the active subject and use short, large, high-contrast labels. Use blue for calcium, yellow for electrical signals and green for fluorescence. Mark every illustrative view and trace 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: Which of these neurons just fired? Their shapes give little away. But watch what happens when the cells contain a protein that changes how brightly it glows. Now there is a change we can follow.

scenes.visual: Overlay 'Watching Neurons Light Up' in the safe frame as the schematic field gently zooms into the cell that brightened. Carry the cell into the next scene.

scenes.tts: Start with that cell. An electrical pulse called a spike opens channels, which are gates that let calcium enter. Calcium inside the cell body stays raised for a while after the pulse has passed.
scenes.caption: Start with that cell. An electrical pulse called a spike opens channels, which are gates that let calcium enter. Calcium inside the cell body stays raised for a while after the pulse has passed.
scenes.visual: Enlarge the schematic cell body in place. Send a yellow pulse along its edge, swing a simple gate open in the membrane and move blue calcium markers through. Let the pulse vanish first while the blue markers continue drifting inside.
scenes.narration: Start with that cell. An electrical pulse called a spike opens channels, which are gates that let calcium enter. Calcium inside the cell body stays raised for a while after the pulse has passed.

scenes.visual: Continue the schematic close-up after the electrical pulse has passed. Keep the blue calcium drifting in the cell body. Drift inward toward the faint green glow to lead into the indicator.

scenes.tts: The protein that makes this rise visible is a calcium indicator called G camp. When calcium binds, part of the protein closes a gap. That keeps water away from the part that gives off light, so the protein shines brighter.
scenes.caption: The protein that makes this rise visible is a calcium indicator called GCaMP. When calcium binds, part of the protein closes a gap. That keeps water away from the part that gives off light, so the protein shines brighter.
scenes.visual: Magnify the same green glow into an abstract schematic indicator icon, a light spot with a simple sliding hatch. As a calcium marker reaches the icon, slide the hatch shut. Drifting water stops at the hatch and the spot brightens. Use a diagrammatic icon with no molecular geometry.
scenes.narration: The protein that makes this rise visible is a calcium indicator called GCaMP. When calcium binds, part of the protein closes a gap. That keeps water away from the part that gives off light, so the protein shines brighter.

scenes.tts: Calcium imaging follows electrical activity by measuring the light from changes in calcium. First measure the brightness before the response. Subtract that starting brightness from the current brightness, then divide the difference by the starting brightness.
scenes.caption: Calcium imaging follows electrical activity by measuring the light from changes in calcium. First measure the brightness before the response. Subtract that starting brightness from the current brightness, then divide the difference by the starting brightness.
scenes.visual: Zoom back into the schematic cell view. Sample its green glow in a pixel window and extend that window into an unnumbered brightness trace. Hold the starting level as a horizontal reference. Pull a bracket between current and starting levels as the narrator says to subtract. Move that bracket above the starting-level swatch in a fraction and reveal '(Current − Start) / Start'.
scenes.narration: Calcium imaging follows electrical activity by measuring the light from changes in calcium. First measure the brightness before the response. Subtract that starting brightness from the current brightness, then divide the difference by the starting brightness.

scenes.tts: The trace now shows how much the light changes relative to where it started. As the cell brightens, the line rises above zero. As the glow fades, the line comes back down.
scenes.caption: The trace now shows how much the light changes relative to where it started. As the cell brightens, the line rises above zero. As the glow fades, the line comes back down.
scenes.visual: Carry the same schematic cell and trace. Turn the fraction into the trace's vertical readout, with a baseline labelled 'No change (0)'. Sweep a time cursor as the green cell brightens and dims and the line rises and returns. Place the trace next to that cell as the field pulls back.
scenes.narration: The trace now shows how much the light changes relative to where it started. As the cell brightens, the line rises above zero. As the glow fades, the line comes back down.

scenes.visual: Let the schematic time cursor glide through the rise and fall in the green trace while the cell glow follows in sync. Leave the 'No change (0)' baseline in place until the cursor has passed the response.

scenes.tts: A microscope can keep the glow from each cell separate, so you can see where activity changes. An optical fibre can collect light from a whole group of cells together. That shared readout is called fibre photometry.
scenes.caption: A microscope can keep the glow from each cell separate, so you can see where activity changes. An optical fibre can collect light from a whole group of cells together. That shared readout is called fibre photometry.
scenes.visual: Pull back to the opening schematic field. Keep the green patch from each visible cell in its own place as the microscope collects the light. Then slide a fibre tip over the same group and show the green contributions feeding one moving glow at the fibre output.
scenes.narration: A microscope can keep the glow from each cell separate, so you can see where activity changes. An optical fibre can collect light from a whole group of cells together. That shared readout is called fibre photometry.

scenes.visual: In the schematic field, gently sweep attention along the green light paths from the cells into the fibre output. Then ease the field back toward the cell that started the film.

scenes.tts: Now return to one cell and watch it fire again while the calcium signal is still fading. Will the light show two separate flashes, or will the responses run together in one swell?
scenes.caption: Now return to one cell and watch it fire again while the calcium signal is still fading. Will the light show two separate flashes, or will the responses run together in one swell?
scenes.visual: Withdraw the fibre and focus on the same schematic cell body. Place two close yellow spike marks above the green readout and show only the fading response to the first. Stop at the second spike and cover the rest of the green trace with a question mark. Show the prompt 'Separate flashes or one swell?'
scenes.narration: Now return to one cell and watch it fire again while the calcium signal is still fading. Will the light show two separate flashes, or will the responses run together in one swell?

scenes.visual: Hold the schematic cell, spike marks, masked portion of the trace and 'Separate flashes or one swell?' for the thinking pause. Keep the answer covered.

scenes.tts: The responses can run together. The indicator brightens and fades slowly compared with the electrical pulse. The next spike can add to the signal that's still fading. A single swell can therefore contain several spikes.
scenes.caption: The responses can run together. The indicator brightens and fades slowly compared with the electrical pulse. The next spike can add to the signal that's still fading. A single swell can therefore contain several spikes.
scenes.visual: Remove the question mark. Scrub over the aligned schematic traces. Let the green curve start to fall after the first yellow spike, rise again from that level after the next and then fade. Let the green glow inside the cell follow the curve.
scenes.narration: The responses can run together. The indicator brightens and fades slowly compared with the electrical pulse. The next spike can add to the signal that's still fading. A single swell can therefore contain several spikes.

scenes.tts: To check which spikes the glow can pick up, record the cell's electrical activity while you film it. Line up both records in time. That comparison tells you what the light can resolve under the conditions you tested.
scenes.caption: To check which spikes the glow can pick up, record the cell's electrical activity while you film it. Line up both records in time. That comparison tells you what the light can resolve under the conditions you tested.
scenes.visual: Draw an electrical recording lead into view alongside the cell and keep the microscope on it. Show the lead feeding the upper yellow trace and the microscope feeding the green trace below. Move a shared time cursor through the schematic recordings so the spikes and their overlapping optical response line up.
scenes.narration: To check which spikes the glow can pick up, record the cell's electrical activity while you film it. Line up both records in time. That comparison tells you what the light can resolve under the conditions you tested.

scenes.visual: Carry the schematic electrical and light records through a moving time window together. Keep each yellow spike visible as the green rise plays out beneath it. Pull outward through the microscope field for the next specimen.

scenes.tts: Across many cells, brightness patterns can show which cells respond alike. In twenty sixteen, Baden and colleagues imaged isolated mouse retinas.
scenes.caption: Across many cells, brightness patterns can show which cells respond alike. In 2016, Baden and colleagues imaged isolated mouse retinas.
scenes.visual: Pull back inside the microscope view and label the new schematic preparation 'Mouse retina'. Show a light stimulus at the edge of the field and let cells brighten in different patterns over time.
scenes.narration: Across many cells, brightness patterns can show which cells respond alike. In 2016, Baden and colleagues imaged isolated mouse retinas.

scenes.tts: They studied the retina's output neurons, called ganglion cells. Grouping cells by how they respond to light defines functional types. They distinguished at least thirty two types.
scenes.caption: They studied the retina's output neurons, called ganglion cells. Grouping cells by how they respond to light defines functional types. They distinguished at least 32 types.
scenes.visual: Keep the schematic retina in frame and draw out a few representative traces from its cells. Slide similar response shapes together and reveal 'At least 32 types' as the narrator gives the finding. The visible sample traces are schematic and do not depict the full count.
scenes.narration: They studied the retina's output neurons, called ganglion cells. Grouping cells by how they respond to light defines functional types. They distinguished at least 32 types.

scenes.tts: You can also ask what makes each cell respond. In twenty fifteen, Barretto and colleagues imaged a cluster of taste neurons, the geniculate ganglion, in anaesthetized mice. Taste solutions flowed over the tongue. Most responding neurons were strongly activated by only one of the tested taste qualities.
scenes.caption: You can also ask what makes each cell respond. In 2015, Barretto and colleagues imaged a cluster of taste neurons, the geniculate ganglion, in anaesthetized mice. Taste solutions flowed over the tongue. Most responding neurons were strongly activated by only one of the tested taste qualities.
scenes.visual: Clear the retinal responses and switch the schematic view to deep-tissue taste neurons in an anaesthetized mouse, viewed through a thin relay lens. Use a schematic inset of solution flowing over the anaesthetized mouse's tongue and mark the new field 'Taste neurons'. Cycle through unnamed taste solutions, clearing the previous response at each switch. Most of the responding illustrative cells glow strongly on just one trial across the cycle. End on the field with a green glow still fading.
scenes.narration: You can also ask what makes each cell respond. In 2015, Barretto and colleagues imaged a cluster of taste neurons, the geniculate ganglion, in anaesthetized mice. Taste solutions flowed over the tongue. Most responding neurons were strongly activated by only one of the tested taste qualities.

scenes.visual: Keep the schematic field gently receding behind the end card in high-contrast text: 'Calcium imaging turns calcium changes into light to track neural activity.'
